stimulus.title: Metals in solutions
stimulus.html: A student places a strip of tin metal, Sn, into a beaker of colorless AgNO₃(aq). After an hour, shiny gray crystals of silver have grown on the strip and the strip is thinner. A second strip of tin placed in Zn(NO₃)₂(aq) shows no change. Tin forms Sn²⁺ ions in these reactions.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write the balanced net ionic equation for the reaction of tin with silver nitrate solution.

rubric.point: Sn(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq) → Sn²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s), balanced for atoms and charge, with no nitrate.

parts.sample: Sn(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq) → Sn²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s). Nitrate is a spectator, and the charge is +2 on each side.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Identify the oxidizing agent in the reaction in part (a). Justify your answer in terms of electrons.

rubric.point: Identifies Ag⁺ as the oxidizing agent because it gains electrons (is reduced, +1 → 0), taking them from tin.
accept: Ag⁺, since it gains an electron each

parts.sample: Ag⁺ is the oxidizing agent. Each Ag⁺ gains one electron and is reduced to Ag (oxidation number +1 to 0); by taking electrons from tin, it causes tin to be oxidized.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Write the oxidation and reduction half-reactions and explain why the coefficient of Ag⁺ in part (a) must be 2.

rubric.point: Gives Sn → Sn²⁺ + 2e⁻ and Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag, and explains that the silver half-reaction must be doubled so electrons lost (2) equal electrons gained.
accept: two Ag⁺ are needed to take the two electrons from one Sn

parts.sample: Oxidation: Sn(s) → Sn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻. Reduction: Ag⁺(aq) + e⁻ → Ag(s). Each tin atom loses two electrons but each Ag⁺ gains only one, so two Ag⁺ are needed per tin atom to make electrons lost equal electrons gained.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Using both observations, rank tin, silver and zinc in order of how readily they lose electrons, and justify the position of tin.

rubric.point: Zn > Sn > Ag, justified: tin gives electrons to Ag⁺ (so loses them more readily than silver) but not to Zn²⁺ (so less readily than zinc).

parts.sample: Zn > Sn > Ag. Tin reduces Ag⁺, so tin gives up electrons more readily than silver. Tin does not reduce Zn²⁺, so it gives up electrons less readily than zinc.
